game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Having followed this game for a while, waiting for the episodes to release, and meeting the devs at PAX, I can say that this was probably one of the most unique "point and click" experiences I've ever had. I can't even go into much detail, because I truly want you to experience this game for yourself, but there are a few things I will say:

+The game really does a good job of making the in-game world feel "real". From a terse, yet thorough, well-thought explanation to "The Nation's" geopolitcal standing, to the online advertisements and clickbait filler that often pepper the relevant articles

+All of the characters have very distinct, memorable lives, and you'll have a chance to explore each and every one of them. There are no characters which get passed over, and this really drives home the point that what you're doing is very 1984. You're not just seeing information relevant to your case, you're seeing ALL of the information.

+The audio. There is, quite frankly, very little music or ambient noise in the game, but this is actually a positive point for this title. Whenever you come across a particularly shocking datachunk, this intense riff plays, and maintains itself until you move on. I often found myself hearing the music before I realized what I was actually looking at, and it made me super excited to keep reading.

-The episodes did feel rather short, despite there being a lot of content in each. This is offset by the fact that you're not paying per episode. When you buy the game, you get the whole game, not just episode one.

-There was a mechanic near the end (not a spoiler), where you are given a limit on how many data chunks you could upload, given the explanation that "as you know, datachunks cost time". This was never really well illustrated in earlier episodes, and, while you were scolded for uploading silly or irrelevant information (such as Cassandra's location being "over the rainbow and into wonderland" in the first episode), you were never really penalized at all unless you uploaded the incorrect answer for a conflicting (yellow) datachunk. I think the entire "limited datachunk" mechanic could have been implemented a bit better, since the player was previously unprepared to deal with that. I think that perhaps an actual time limit (via countdown timer) would have made the whole thing seem a bit more frenzied, instead of the player idly dawdling, and having time to carefully consider their decisions.


All in all, this was a great game, and I seriously look forward to seeing more great ideas come out of this developer!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Welcome to Orwell, the game where you're just an investigator, and a god. 
Collected information has consequences, mild and severe. 

The game is immersive, pulling you into this fascinating story with plot twists emerging from almost every drag of information. 
There is no hunt for information though, it is more or less given to you. One can argue that due to the long texts it makes the game easier and more of a story game, which I agree to. But on the other hand, I would really enjoy to actually "hunt" for information, having more strict time limits for tapping into phone calls, chats, and computers. Controls are easily understood, music is soooooo fitting and good (but repetitive), and the story is more interesting the more you read.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A wonderful game.

Orwell has rich story and plenty of twists and turns, making it as enjoyable as reading a novel whereas one would be able to participate in the story.  

It is kinda like Papers, Please, yet not as challenging in its gameplay, which means one would be able to put more attention to the fascination of explore, deduct and decide. There is no time limit, so I could always take time to read over each entry and I like that.

However this game is more like an interactive novel with several main branches of progression. It is understandable that since there are so many contents (or so called "datachunks") featured, the producer of this game just cannot create so many responses for all of them. There are some "datachunks" I had to report even though I meant not to do so. I just had to report them in order to move on.

But overall it is a great game for anyone who love stories in game.

Would certainly play to find other endings in the future.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Let me start with saying this: 
This game is creepy AF, if you think about it deeply. Orwell was right, even in 1948 (or 1984, depends on how you want to look at it).

Initially you're searching for details about Oleg Bakay, a missing military officer from neighboring country Parges. Soon--and for the remainder of the game--your focus shifts to Raban Vhart, a blogger whose anti-government sentiments and campaign against the leadership of The Nation (which is, yes, run by a man who looks a bit like Trump) must be thwarted. You are, essentially, the bad guy, running surveillance for a dictatorship that demands absolute fealty from the citizens it so closely monitors, but Ignorance is Strength is less explicit about the meaning behind all of this than the first game was. While Orwell stretched across five episodic instalments, Ignorance is Strength runs for just three, which winds up being too little time to build upon the previously established mythology of the game's world. The broader political climate of The Nation, the appropriately Orwellian setting for both games, isn't expanded upon much by Raban's war against it, and while a conflict with Parges is discussed it's never quite explored enough to feel like a proper plot point.

Your job is to find chunks of data online using the computer interface of the Orwell surveillance system, then throw as much dirt as you can at Raban. If a piece of information on a page can be collected, it will be highlighted, and you can drag it to their profile on your screen. You find this information by scouring websites (although annoyingly you can't "search" for sites; you either find links on sites you have already accessed or gain a new site for your database after grabbing a data chunk), and when you manage to find someone's phone or computer details you can snoop through their private screens too. Pages that haven't been fully explored, or which have data chunks you haven't lifted, are highlighted on your list of pages visited. Each piece of information you collect will eat up ten minutes on your in-game clock, and in each of the game's three episodes you're working towards a specific time limit, so you want to focus on the important information and skip over any data that does not add to the case you're building.

Sometimes data will contradict with other chunks, and as the Investigator it's up to you to choose which one to submit. The "Ethical Codex" mandate means that your supervisor is only privy to information you submit, and will make informed decisions based on that. The way the plot progresses will be influenced by which statements you decide are more valid, as you can't submit two contradictory pieces. It's an implausible system, but from a game design perspective it's a clever one, forcing you into regular moral dilemmas.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

The obvious limitation is that you can't make recommendations. Your ability to control and shape the situation comes from the data you do or, often more crucially, don't upload. Orwell teaches this lesson early on, when a target jokes about stealing her boyfriend's credit card. Upload that data chunk and Symes, who can't see the playful dynamic of the relationship, has the card cancelled. In later episodes, the stakes are more dramatic. There are some major decisions that can have a profound effect on the story—albeit, as is often the case with episodic storytelling, the story follows the same major beats no matter your choices. But doing what seems like the noble thing doesn't always lead to the best outcome. It's complicated and messy, which feels right.

Despite these problems, Orwell is a success. It lets you watch over a spiralling conspiratorial thriller, and throws in enough twists and surprises to keep things interesting. It's an enjoyable way to interact with a world—the voyeurism creating a distinct, enjoyable power dynamic that I refuse to self-reflect on any further. It's not at all subtle—it's called Orwell, after all—but it's a well told mystery framed by a captivating storytelling device.

The story telling was amazing, tho a bit too *I am waiting for an animation to skip* 
It was fun, but definitely deserves to be played with time and clear mind. 
Now if you will excuse me, I will try to disconnect from Orwell

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An interesting puzzle/story game with a heavy-handed message.

Gameplay revolves around using a web-browser-like interface to look for information on persons of interest.  The interface is completely adequate for that purpose and that's about all you can say about the mechanics of the game.  

I'm not sure that the game has a Lose-State so you're essentially free to do whatever you want which is cool.  Personally, I'd have liked a few more red herrings or maybe a thing where my handler buddy gets weirded out while I obsessively upload as many pictures of everyone that I could find.  Also, I enjoyed the time limit aspect of one part of the game and seeing that in other places would have been cool.

The story and writing do all the heavy lifting for the game and I feel like it did a good job.  The scenario is fairly realistic and the characters are written well enough that you can get a feel for what's going on without things feeling too obvious, contrived, or arbitrary... except for one thing: there is an ending that (as far as I can tell) is entirely missing from the game and it feels like a missed opportunity to not allow players to pursue it.  I'm sure it's entirely intentional but I disagree with it.

Anyhow, the game's got 5 episodes and each of those take about an hour to complete.  I'd say it's well worth it if you can pick it up for 10bux or less.

review_text_raw:
Replaying a story-driven little-actual-gameplay game is a rare occurrence for me, let alone replaying it immediately after the first time, and yet I did it here since I felt that it would have enough replayability to stand up, and it did. 

Chats and phone calls move fast enough to make adding datachunks awkward, but too slow otherwise, especially the second time through them when you already know what everyone is going to say. While one conversation is under a time limit, the rest could use a fast-forward button.

The game is very short. I have 6 hours on record and that's from playing through the game in its entirety twice, including some idle time when I walked away from the computer. Some players may not find the amount of content acceptable considering the price.

By far the biggest issue is that [spoiler]Orwell is essentially introduced and dismantled within the game world during the course of the game. While that is obviously relevant to the plot and its general message, I can't help but feel that there's potential for multiple cases using this "engine", for lack of a better word, so it's a shame that, narratively, that can't occur,[/spoiler] although the fact that I find that in particular to be the largest issue is a very good thing for this game.
